title: Understanding Biogeographic Patterns in Sepiolidae (Cephalopoda)
content:
ABSTRACT

The biogeography of the bobtail squid family Sepiolidae is reviewed. Species of the Sepiolinae subfamily are only found in coastal waters of the ‘Old World’, with a high degree of diversification in the Mediterranean Sea and the Coral Triangle in the Indo-Pacific region. The Rossiinae subfamily inhabits coasts of both the Old and New Worlds. Finally, the Heteroteuthinae subfamily exhibits widespread distribution patterns in the oceans of the whole world. The Mediterranean and Coral Triangle waters correspond to hotspots of biodiversity for the family, with 24.1% and 19.0% of the species, respectively, and with a high predominance of Sepiolinae species (17.7% and 13.9%) compared to Rossiinae (2.5% and 1.3%) and Heteroteuthinae (3.8% and 3.8%). The Sepiolinae species inhabit shallow, coastal, benthic habitats, and their paralarvae have a nectobenthic paralarvae strategy with a planktonic stage limited in time, which quickly adopts the benthic lifestyle. The Rossiinae species are adapted to benthic habitats in deeper waters on continental shelves and slopes. They lay large eggs, and the newly hatchlings have a Direct Nectobenthic Juvenile strategy, adopting a benthic lifestyle with only a very brief, if any, planktonic stage. Heteroteuthinae species occupy pelagic habitats, lay small eggs associated to seamounts, islands and continental slopes and give birth to hatchlings that adopt a pelagic paralarvae strategy with a planktonic larval stage. The biogeographic patterns of the Sepiolidae family show the remarkable adaptability of this group to both coastal and oceanic environments. However, some species still have unknown distribution patterns and are seemingly cryptic. Understanding these biogeographical patterns is a useful tool for identifying potential cryptic species and, consequently, for improving the management of conservation measures for species affected by phenomena such as climate change.
